questions.q: What is the peak age of incidence for Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) in pediatric patients?
options: A) 2 to 5 years of age (with a peak incidence at 3 years)
B) Less than 6 months of age
C) 10 to 14 years of age
D) 15 to 18 years of age
questions.hint: Most common between 2 and 5 years, peaking at age 3.
questions.explanation: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) is predominantly diagnosed in early childhood, with the vast majority of cases occurring between 2 and 5 years of age and peaking at age 3.

questions.q: From which embryological tissue origin does Nephroblastoma arise within the kidney?
options: A) Adrenal cortical zona fasciculata
B) Persistent nephrogenic blastema (metanephric blastema)
C) Transformed vascular endothelial cells of Bowman's capsule
D) Transitional cell epithelium of the renal pelvis
questions.hint: Persistent nephrogenic (metanephric) blastema.
questions.explanation: Nephroblastoma is an embryonal malignant renal tumor arising from persistent, dysplastic embryonal renal tissue known as metanephric blastema.

questions.q: What cell line of origin gives rise to Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Renal tubular epithelial cells
B) Splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages
C) Neural crest cells of the sympathetic nervous system
D) Skeletal muscle satellite cells
questions.hint: Neural crest cells of the sympathetic nervous system.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma is an embryonal neoplasm that originates from primordial neural crest cells destined to form the sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla.

questions.q: What is the single most frequent anatomical primary site for Neuroblastoma development in children?
options: A) Posterior fossa of the brain
B) Distal anterior mediastinum
C) Subcutaneous tissue of the thigh
D) Adrenal medulla (accounting for ~50% of primary cases)
questions.hint: Adrenal medulla (~50% of primary cases).
questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla is the most common anatomical site of origin for neuroblastoma, giving rise to approximately 50% of all primary tumors, followed by the retroperitoneal sympathetic chain.

questions.q: What is the classic physical presentation of an abdominal mass in a child with Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor)?
options: A) A smooth, firm, non-tender intra-renal mass that stays strictly unilateral and does NOT cross the midline
B) A hard, nodular, fixed abdominal mass that freely crosses the aortic midline
C) A soft, diffusely tender, fluctuating mass extending into the inguinal canal
D) A small hyper-pulsatile vascular mass located in the epigastrium
questions.hint: Smooth, firm, unilateral intra-renal mass that does not cross the midline.
questions.explanation: Wilms tumor typically presents as a smooth, firm, non-tender flank mass originating within the renal capsule that expands unilaterally without crossing the abdominal midline.

questions.q: In contrast to Wilms tumor, what are the physical examination characteristics of the abdominal mass in Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Soft, cystic, mobile, and non-palpable
B) Hard, irregular, nodular, fixed, and frequently crossing the abdominal midline
C) Smooth, uniform, non-fixed, and strictly localized to the pelvis
D) Bounding, compressible, and localized to the anterior abdominal wall
questions.hint: Hard, irregular/nodular, fixed, and frequently crosses the midline.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma masses originate from retroperitoneal sympathetic chain or adrenal tissue, typically presenting as hard, fixed, irregular/nodular structures that cross the anatomical midline.

questions.q: Which diagnostic tumor suppressor gene, located on chromosome 11p13, is directly linked to the development of Wilms tumor?
options: A) MYCN gene
B) RB1 gene
C) WT1 gene
D) TP53 gene
questions.hint: WT1 on chromosome 11p13.
questions.explanation: The WT1 gene (Wilms Tumor 1), mapped to chromosome 11p13, plays a critical role in normal renal and gonadal embryogenesis and is mutated or deleted in Wilms tumor cases.

questions.q: What percentage of children with Neuroblastoma present with metastatic disease at the time of initial diagnosis?
options: A) Less than 5%
B) Approximately 15%
C) Approximately 35%
D) Over 70%
questions.hint: Over 70% already have metastases at diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma is a biologically aggressive malignancy; more than 70% of affected children present with widespread metastatic disease (to bone marrow, bones, liver, or lymph nodes) at initial presentation.

questions.q: What urinary catecholamine metabolites are pathognomonic markers elevated in over 90% of Neuroblastoma patients?
options: A) Homovanillic acid (HVA) and Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
B) 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) and Serotonin
C) Uric acid and Creatinine
D) Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and Beta-hCG
questions.hint: Urinary HVA and VMA.
questions.explanation: Because neuroblastoma cells synthesize and metabolize catecholamines, >90% of patients excrete elevated urinary levels of Homovanillic Acid (HVA) and Vanillylmandelic Acid (VMA).

questions.q: What is the overall cure rate for children diagnosed with Favorable Histology Wilms Tumor under modern multi-disciplinary protocols?
options: A) Less than 20%
B) Greater than 90%
C) Exactly 50%
questions.hint: Over 90% cure rate for favorable histology.
questions.explanation: Favorable histology Wilms tumor has one of the highest cure rates in pediatric oncology, exceeding 90% when managed with combined surgery and chemotherapy.

questions.q: Which congenital syndrome features the combination of Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, and Range of mental retardation (intellectual disability)?
options: A) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
B) Denys-Drash syndrome
C) WAGR syndrome
D) Li-Fraumeni syndrome
questions.hint: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, and Range of mental retardation = WAGR.
questions.explanation: WAGR syndrome is a classic contiguous gene deletion syndrome on chromosome 11p13 characterized by Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, and Range of mental retardation.

questions.q: What clinical triad of features characterizes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, a genetic condition predisposing to Wilms tumor?
options: A) Microcephaly, cleft lip, and polydactyly
B) Aniridia, hypospadias, and renal failure
C) Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart defect
D) Macrosomia, Omphalocele (exomphalos), and Macroglossia (often with hemihypertrophy and neonatal hypoglycemia)
questions.hint: Macrosomia, omphalocele, and macroglossia.
questions.explanation: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15 locus) presents with overgrowth features: macrosomia, omphalocele, macroglossia, ear creases, hemihypertrophy, and an increased risk of Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.

questions.q: Which oncogene amplification (located on chromosome 2p24) serves as the most critical independent marker of poor prognosis in Neuroblastoma?
options: A) MYCN amplification
B) BCR::ABL1 fusion
C) FLT3-ITD mutation
D) ETV6::RUNX1 translocation
questions.hint: MYCN amplification (chromosome 2p24).
questions.explanation: MYCN gene amplification (>10 copies) occurs in ~20% of neuroblastomas and strongly correlates with rapid tumor progression, treatment resistance, and poor prognosis regardless of patient age or stage.

questions.q: What physical examination sign describes periorbital ecchymosis and proptosis secondary to orbital bone metastases in Neuroblastoma?
options: A) 'Blueberry muffin' skin lesions
B) 'Raccoon eyes'
C) 'Dewdrops on a rose petal'
D) 'Strawberry nevus'
questions.hint: Orbital metastases cause 'raccoon eyes'.
questions.explanation: Metastatic neuroblastoma infiltration into the retrobulbar orbital bones and surrounding tissues causes periorbital ecchymosis and proptosis, clinically recognized as 'raccoon eyes'.

questions.q: What is Pepper Syndrome in neonatal/infantile Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Bilateral adrenal calcification causing acute Addisonian crisis
B) Intra-spinal extension causing acute paraplegia
C) Massive liver metastasis in infants causing severe hepatomegaly and respiratory compromise
D) Chronic secretory diarrhea secondary to VIP secretion
questions.hint: Massive liver metastasis in infants.
questions.explanation: Pepper syndrome describes extensive metastatic dissemination of neuroblastoma to the liver in infants, causing massive hepatomegaly that compresses the lungs and inferior vena cava.

questions.q: What paraneoplastic autoimmune syndrome associated with Neuroblastoma presents with rapid chaotic eye movements, rhythmic muscle twitching, and ataxia?
options: A) Horner syndrome
B) Cushing syndrome
C) WAGR syndrome
D) Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome (OMAS)
questions.hint: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMAS).
questions.explanation: Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome (OMAS / 'dancing eyes, dancing feet') is a paraneoplastic autoimmune condition triggered by neuroblastoma, featuring opsoclonus, myoclonus, and cerebellar ataxia.

questions.q: Under the SIOP (International Society of Paediatric Oncology) protocol used in Tanzania and Europe for Wilms tumor, what is the mandatory initial management step?
options: A) Pre-operative chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin D) for 4 to 6 weeks FIRST to shrink the tumor before surgery
B) Immediate radical nephrectomy on the day of admission
C) Immediate total body irradiation
D) High-dose oral corticosteroids for 6 months
questions.hint: Pre-operative chemotherapy (vincristine + actinomycin D) before nephrectomy.
questions.explanation: The SIOP protocol administers pre-operative chemotherapy (Vincristine + Actinomycin D) to reduce tumor volume and downstage the lesion prior to nephrectomy, minimizing the risk of intraoperative tumor rupture.

questions.q: How is Unfavorable Histology Wilms tumor defined microscopically?
options: A) Presence of uniform mature tubular structures
B) Presence of nuclear Anaplasia (marked nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and multipolar mitotic figures)
C) Abundant fibroblastic stroma without epithelial cells
D) Complete absence of cell mitosis
questions.hint: Nuclear anaplasia defines unfavorable histology.
questions.explanation: Unfavorable histology in Wilms tumor is defined by the presence of nuclear anaplasia (bizarre pleomorphic giant nuclei, hyperchromasia, atypical multipolar mitoses), which confers chemoresistance.

questions.q: Which rare clinical manifestation of Neuroblastoma occurs due to tumor secretion of Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP)?
options: A) Severe hypertension and bradycardia
B) Polycythemia and facial flushing
C) Kerner-Morrison syndrome (profuse, watery secretory diarrhea with severe hypokalemia)
D) Acute renal failure with hyperuricemia
questions.hint: VIP secretion causes watery diarrhea and hypokalemia (Kerner-Morrison syndrome).
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma tumor cells can secrete Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP), causing intractable watery diarrhea, electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia), and metabolic acidosis (Kerner-Morrison syndrome).

questions.q: What specific neurological sign occurs when a thoracic or cervical Neuroblastoma involves the sympathetic stellate ganglion?
options: A) Bell's palsy
B) Parotid enlargement
C) Nystagmus and papilledema
D) Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, and enophthalmos)
questions.hint: Sympathetic chain involvement causes Horner syndrome.
questions.explanation: Compression or invasion of the cervical/thoracic sympathetic chain by neuroblastoma produces ipsilateral Horner syndrome, characterized by ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, and enophthalmos.

questions.q: According to the SIOP / NWTSG staging systems for Wilms Tumor, what defines Stage I disease?
options: A) Tumor limited strictly to the kidney, intact capsule, completely resected without rupture or residual tumor
B) Tumor extending beyond the kidney into retroperitoneal fat but completely excised
C) Tumor spillage into the abdominal cavity during surgery or regional lymph node involvement
D) Presence of hematogenous metastases to the lungs or liver
questions.hint: Confined to the kidney with an intact capsule and complete excision.
questions.explanation: Stage I Wilms tumor is strictly limited to the kidney, with an intact pseudo-capsule, no vessel invasion, and complete surgical excision with clear margins.

questions.q: What defines Stage III Wilms Tumor in surgical staging?
options: A) Unilateral tumor completely excised with negative margins
B) Residual non-hematogenous tumor confined to the abdomen (e.g., regional lymph node involvement, tumor spillage during surgery, or peritoneal implants)
C) Distant blood-borne metastases to lungs, liver, or bone
D) Synchronous bilateral renal involvement
questions.hint: Residual non-hematogenous abdominal tumor (lymph nodes, spillage, or implants).
questions.explanation: Stage III Wilms tumor involves residual non-hematogenous tumor within the abdomen, including positive regional lymph nodes, intraoperative spillage, peritoneal seeding, or incomplete surgical resection.

questions.q: What defines Stage V Wilms Tumor at initial presentation?
options: A) Unresectable retroperitoneal tumor crossing the midline
B) Solitary lung metastasis
C) Bilateral renal involvement at the time of initial diagnosis
D) Recurrent tumor 2 years post-treatment
questions.hint: Bilateral renal involvement at diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Stage V Wilms tumor is defined by synchronous or metachronous involvement of both kidneys at initial diagnosis, requiring renal-sparing treatment strategies.

questions.q: Why do approximately 25% of children with Nephroblastoma develop systemic Hypertension at presentation?
options: A) Excess secretion of epinephrine by metanephric blastema
B) Direct tumor invasion into the adrenal cortex
C) Co-existing coarctation of the aorta
D) Renal ischemia caused by tumor compression of intra-renal arteries, stimulating the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone Axis
questions.hint: Renal ischemia activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
questions.explanation: Wilms tumor expansion compresses adjacent renal parenchyma and blood vessels, inducing intra-renal ischemia that triggers excessive renin secretion and hypertension.

questions.q: Under the International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS), how is Stage 3 Neuroblastoma defined?
options: A) Unresectable unilateral tumor crossing the midline, or localized unilateral tumor with contralateral regional lymph node involvement
B) Completely resected localized tumor with negative lymph nodes
C) Metastases restricted to skin and liver in infants <1 year
D) Distant bone marrow involvement in a 5-year-old
questions.hint: Unresectable tumor crossing midline or contralateral regional lymph nodes.
questions.explanation: INSS Stage 3 Neuroblastoma includes unresectable primary tumors extending across the midline (with or without regional lymph node involvement) or unilateral tumors with positive contralateral lymph nodes.

questions.q: What unique clinical behavior defines Stage 4S (INSS) / Stage MS (INRG) Neuroblastoma in infants under 12–18 months of age?
options: A) Rapid fatal progression despite intensive multi-agent chemotherapy
B) High rate of spontaneous regression with minimal or no cytotoxic chemotherapy
C) Universal transformation into high-grade osteosarcoma
D) Exclusive metastasis to the central nervous system parenchyma
questions.hint: High rate of spontaneous regression.
questions.explanation: Stage 4S (special) neuroblastoma occurs in infants <1 year with localized primary tumor and metastases limited to liver, skin, and/or <10% bone marrow. It uniquely undergoes high rates of spontaneous regression, yielding survival >80–90%.

questions.q: What physical finding indicates intra-spinal extension ('dumbbell tumor') of a paraspinal Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Palpable thrill over the epigastrium
B) Macroglossia and omphalocele
C) Neurological deficits such as progressive lower extremity weakness, loss of bowel/bladder control, or paraplegia
D) Bilateral undescended testes
questions.hint: Spinal cord compression causes leg weakness, sensory/sphincter changes, or paraplegia.
questions.explanation: Paraspinal neuroblastomas can grow through neural foramina into the spinal canal ('dumbbell tumor'), compressing the spinal cord and causing nerve root pain, leg weakness, and sphincter dysfunction.

questions.q: What microscopic appearance characterizes the classic histopathology of triphasic Wilms Tumor?
options: A) Uniform sheet of mature histiocytes with lipid vacuoles
B) Multinucleated Reed-Sternberg cells surrounded by lymphocytes
C) Interlocking bundles of smooth muscle fibers without mitosis
D) Triphasic combination of Blastemal, Epithelial (tubules/glomeruloid structures), and Stromal elements
questions.hint: Blastemal, epithelial, and stromal components.
questions.explanation: Classic Wilms tumor exhibits a triphasic histologic pattern composed of undifferentiated blastema, epithelial structures (primitive tubules or glomeruli), and mesenchymal stroma.

questions.q: What histological feature is characteristic of Neuroblastoma tissue on routine microscopic examination?
options: A) Homer-Wright pseudorosettes (tumor cells arranged around a central meshwork of neural fibers)
B) 'Starry sky' pattern of macrophages ingesting apoptotic debris
C) Auer rods inside cell cytoplasm
D) Concentric calcified psammoma bodies
questions.hint: Homer-Wright pseudorosettes.
questions.explanation: Neuroblastoma microscopy shows small round blue cells forming Homer-Wright pseudorosettes (rings of tumor cell nuclei surrounding a central fibrillar neuropil core).

questions.q: Which serum laboratory markers correlate with high tumor burden and poor prognosis in Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Elevated serum amylase and lipase
B) Elevated Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) and serum Ferritin
C) Decreased serum uric acid
D) Elevated alkaline phosphatase alone
questions.hint: Elevated LDH and serum ferritin.
questions.explanation: High serum Ferritin (>145 ng/mL) and elevated Serum LDH (>1500 U/L) reflect massive tumor cell turnover and high body tumor burden in neuroblastoma, correlating with advanced stage and inferior survival.

questions.q: On abdominal Cross-Sectional CT imaging, what characteristic sign differentiates Wilms Tumor from Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Neuroblastoma originates inside the renal cortex; Wilms tumor originates in the spleen
B) Neuroblastoma never contains calcifications; Wilms tumor contains calcifications in 100% of cases
C) Wilms tumor produces the 'Claw Sign' (compressed normal renal parenchyma wrapping around the intra-renal mass), whereas Neuroblastoma encases and displaces major blood vessels
D) Wilms tumor always crosses the midline and invades the contralateral adrenal gland
questions.hint: Wilms shows the 'claw sign' of renal tissue; neuroblastoma encases vessels.
questions.explanation: CT imaging distinguishes intra-renal Wilms tumor (which stretches normal renal tissue into a 'claw sign') from extra-renal Neuroblastoma (which encases major abdominal vessels and crosses the midline).

questions.q: What nuclear medicine functional imaging scan is highly specific for staging and detecting metastatic Neuroblastoma lesions?
options: A) Technetium-99m bone scan only
B) Gallium-67 scan
C) Positron emission tomography with glucose only
D) Iodine-123 Metaiodobenzylguanidine (123I-MIBG) scan
questions.hint: Iodine-123 MIBG scan.
questions.explanation: MIBG is a structural analog of norepinephrine that is selectively taken up by sympathetic adrenergic tissues, making Iodine-123 MIBG scintigraphy the gold-standard imaging modality for neuroblastoma.

questions.q: What imaging modality is superior for evaluating suspected intra-spinal extension ('dumbbell tumor') in Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
B) Plain abdominal radiograph
C) Renal ultrasound
D) Intravenous pyelogram (IVP)
questions.hint: MRI best shows spinal canal and soft-tissue extension.
questions.explanation: MRI provides superior soft-tissue contrast resolution, making it the definitive modality to evaluate spinal canal patency and spinal cord compression in paraspinal neuroblastoma.

questions.q: What chemotherapy agents constitute the standard pre-operative regimen for Low/Intermediate-Risk Wilms Tumor under the SIOP protocol?
options: A) Cisplatin and Etoposide
B) Vincristine and Actinomycin D
C) Cyclophosphamide and Doxorubicin
D) Methotrexate and Cytarabine
questions.hint: Vincristine and actinomycin D.
questions.explanation: The standard SIOP pre-operative chemotherapy for localized Wilms tumor consists of 4 weeks of Vincristine and Actinomycin D (doxorubicin is added for metastatic or high-risk disease).

questions.q: Why is palpation of the abdomen performed with extreme gentleness or restricted during pre-operative clinical evaluation of suspected Wilms Tumor?
options: A) Palpation causes severe hypokalemia
B) To avoid triggering excessive catecholamine release
C) To prevent accidental rupture of the renal tumor capsule and intra-abdominal tumor spillage (which upgrades stage to Stage III)
D) To prevent dislodgement of cardiac pacemakers
questions.hint: Avoid tumor rupture and spillage, which upgrades the stage to Stage III.
questions.explanation: Vigorous abdominal palpation can rupture the delicate capsule of a Wilms tumor, spilling tumor cells into the peritoneal cavity and upgrading the patient's stage from Stage I/II to Stage III.

questions.q: What biological differentiation therapy agent is administered post-chemotherapy in high-risk Neuroblastoma to eliminate residual microscopic disease?
options: A) All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA)
B) Interferon-alpha
C) Levamisole
D) 13-cis-retinoic acid (Isotretinoin)
questions.hint: 13-cis-retinoic acid (isotretinoin).
questions.explanation: Oral 13-cis-retinoic acid (Isotretinoin) induces terminal differentiation of neuroblastoma blasts and is standard consolidation therapy following high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell rescue.

questions.q: What imaging finding on plain abdominal radiography is present in over 80% of Neuroblastoma cases?
options: A) Fine stippled intratumoral calcifications
B) Double-bubble sign
C) Pneumoperitoneum
D) Ground-glass opacity of the lungs
questions.hint: Fine stippled calcifications inside the tumor.
questions.explanation: Dystrophic calcification within necrotic tumor tissue produces fine, stippled calcifications visible on plain radiographs and CT scans in >80% of neuroblastomas.

questions.q: What is the surgical management strategy for Stage V (Bilateral) Wilms Tumor?
options: A) Bilateral total nephrectomy with immediate lifelong dialysis on Day 1
B) Pre-operative chemotherapy followed by bilateral nephron-sparing (partial) surgery to preserve functional renal parenchyma
C) Radiation therapy to both kidneys without surgery
D) Immediate bilateral renal transplantation
questions.hint: Pre-op chemotherapy followed by nephron-sparing (partial) surgery.
questions.explanation: Stage V Wilms tumor management focuses on preserving renal function: pre-operative chemotherapy shrinks both tumors, followed by partial nephrectomy (nephron-sparing surgery) on both kidneys.

questions.q: Which clinical syndrome predisposing to Wilms tumor features pseudohermaphroditism, early-onset progressive renal failure (diffuse mesangial sclerosis), and Wilms tumor?
options: A) WAGR syndrome
B) Li-Fraumeni syndrome
C) Denys-Drash syndrome
D) Sotos syndrome
questions.hint: Denys-Drash syndrome (WT1 mutation).
questions.explanation: Denys-Drash syndrome (point mutation in WT1) is characterized by the triad of Wilms tumor, male pseudohermaphroditism (genital ambiguity), and progressive nephrotic syndrome due to diffuse mesangial sclerosis.

questions.q: What monoclonal antibody targeting the GD2 disialoganglioside surface antigen is used in modern immunotherapy protocols for high-risk Neuroblastoma?
options: A) Rituximab
B) Blinatumomab
C) Infliximab
D) Dinutuximab (anti-GD2)
questions.hint: Dinutuximab targets GD2.
questions.explanation: Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets GD2, a glycolipid heavily expressed on neuroblastoma cells, significantly improving event-free and overall survival in high-risk neuroblastoma.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with a painless, smooth, firm left flank mass, BP 135/85 mmHg, microscopic hematuria, and an intra-renal mass on CT with a positive 'claw sign' (no calcifications, does not cross midline). Identify the diagnosis, mechanism of hypertension, and initial SIOP management.
options: A) Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor); Intra-renal ischemia stimulating Renin secretion; Administer 4–6 weeks of pre-operative Vincristine + Actinomycin D followed by radical nephrectomy
B) Neuroblastoma; Epinephrine hypersecretion; Perform immediate emergency total hepatectomy
C) Polycystic Kidney Disease; Salt retention; Give high-dose loop diuretics
D) Renal Cell Carcinoma; Erythropoietin surge; Immediate radiation therapy
questions.hint: Smooth intra-renal mass + 'claw sign' + hypertension = Wilms tumor (renin-mediated); SIOP uses pre-op vincristine + actinomycin D before nephrectomy.
questions.explanation: A smooth intra-renal mass in a 3-year-old with hematuria, hypertension (renin-mediated), and a CT 'claw sign' without crossing the midline is classic for Wilms tumor. SIOP protocol initiates treatment with pre-operative Vincristine + Actinomycin D prior to nephrectomy.

questions.q: A 14-month-old infant presents with fever, weight loss, a hard, fixed, nodular abdominal mass crossing the midline, 'raccoon eyes', opsoclonus-myoclonus, high urinary HVA/VMA, and a calcified retroperitoneal mass encasing vessels on CT. Diagnose the condition, tissue of origin, and eye/movement disorder.
options: A) Wilms tumor; Metanephric blastema; WAGR syndrome
B) Neuroblastoma; Neural crest cells of sympathetic ganglia/adrenal medulla; Opsoclonus-Myoclonus-Ataxia Syndrome (paraneoplastic autoimmune response)
C) Burkitt Lymphoma; Mature B-cells; Epstein-Barr virus reaction
D) Retinoblastoma; Retinal progenitor cells; Horner syndrome
questions.hint: Hard midline-crossing mass + raccoon eyes + high HVA/VMA = neuroblastoma from neural crest cells with OMAS.
questions.explanation: An infant with a hard abdominal mass crossing the midline, raccoon eyes, elevated VMA/HVA, and opsoclonus-myoclonus has Neuroblastoma (arising from neural crest cells). Opsoclonus-myoclonus is a pathognomonic paraneoplastic autoimmune syndrome.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with massive hepatomegaly causing retractions, bluish skin nodules ('blueberry muffin' spots), a 1.5 cm left adrenal mass, and 6% neuroblastoma cells in bone marrow. What INSS/INRG stage is this, what is the expected outcome, and what is the primary management?
options: A) Stage 1; Requires total bilateral adrenalectomy
B) Stage 4; Requires intensive multi-agent chemotherapy and stem cell rescue
C) Stage 4S (INSS) / Stage MS (INRG); High rate of spontaneous regression with excellent overall survival (>80–90%); Managed conservatively with supportive care/observation
D) Stage 3; Requires emergency total body irradiation
questions.hint: Infant <1 year with localized tumor + liver/skin/<10% marrow = Stage 4S/MS; high spontaneous regression, mainly observation.
questions.explanation: An infant <1 year with localized primary neuroblastoma and metastases limited to liver, skin, and <10% marrow has Stage 4S / MS. This stage has a remarkable rate of spontaneous regression and is managed primarily with observation.

questions.q: A newborn male has a large omphalocele, macroglossia, birth weight 4.8 kg (macrosomia), right hemihypertrophy, and neonatal hypoglycemia. Name the syndrome, the abdominal tumor to screen for every 3 months until age 8, and the affected chromosome region.
options: A) WAGR syndrome; Retinoblastoma; Chromosome 13q14
B) Denys-Drash syndrome; Neuroblastoma; Chromosome 1p36
C) Sotos syndrome; Medulloblastoma; Chromosome 5q
D) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor); Chromosome 11p15
questions.hint: Omphalocele, macroglossia, macrosomia (11p15) = Beckwith-Wiedemann; screen for Wilms tumor.
questions.explanation: Omphalocele, macroglossia, macrosomia, hemihypertrophy, and hypoglycemia define Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15 locus). Children require 3-monthly abdominal ultrasounds to screen for Wilms tumor.

questions.q: A 4-year-old undergoes radical nephrectomy for a right flank mass with an intact capsule and clear renal margins, but 2 regional para-aortic lymph nodes contain Wilms tumor cells. What is the surgical stage, and is post-operative therapy required?
options: A) Stage III (due to positive regional lymph nodes); Yes, mandates post-operative multi-agent chemotherapy and flank radiation therapy
B) Stage I; No treatment required
C) Stage II; Chemotherapy alone without radiation
D) Stage IV; Palliative care only
questions.hint: Positive regional lymph nodes = Stage III, requiring post-op chemotherapy and flank irradiation.
questions.explanation: Presence of tumor in regional lymph nodes upgrades Wilms tumor to Stage III (regardless of complete local excision), which requires post-operative multi-agent chemotherapy and abdominal radiation therapy.

questions.q: A 2-year-old girl with a thoracic paraspinal Neuroblastoma develops progressive leg weakness, hyperreflexia, and urinary retention over 48 hours, with spine MRI showing extension through the T6-T7 foramen compressing the spinal cord. What is this configuration called, and what is the immediate medical treatment?
options: A) 'Blueberry muffin' tumor; Intravenous high-dose furosemide
B) 'Dumbbell tumor' (intra-spinal extension); High-dose Intravenous Corticosteroids (Dexamethasone) and emergency neurosurgical decompression or chemotherapy
C) 'Claw sign' tumor; Oral aspirin
D) 'Raccoon' tumor; Lumbar puncture
questions.hint: Foraminal/spinal canal extension = 'dumbbell tumor'; urgent IV dexamethasone and decompression/chemotherapy.
questions.explanation: Paraspinal tumors extending through neural foramina into the spinal canal are termed 'dumbbell tumors'. Acute spinal cord compression is a medical emergency managed with high-dose IV Dexamethasone and urgent decompression/chemotherapy.

questions.q: In comparing Wilms Tumor vs Neuroblastoma: which originates from metanephric blastema as a smooth unilateral mass with >90% cure rate, and which originates from neural crest cells as a hard midline-crossing mass with HVA/VMA secretion and MYCN risk?
options: A) 1. Neuroblastoma; 2. Wilms tumor
B) 1. Rhabdomyosarcoma; 2. Hepatoblastoma
C) 1. Wilms tumor (Nephroblastoma); 2. Neuroblastoma
D) 1. Lymphoma; 2. Leukemia
questions.hint: 1. Wilms tumor; 2. Neuroblastoma.
questions.explanation: Wilms tumor originates from metanephric blastema, presents as a smooth unilateral mass not crossing the midline, and has a cure rate >90%. Neuroblastoma originates from neural crest cells, presents as a hard nodular mass crossing the midline, secretes HVA/VMA, and is driven by MYCN amplification.

questions.q: A 3-year-old with high-risk MYCN-amplified abdominal Neuroblastoma completes induction chemotherapy and resection. What consolidation therapy is used, and what differentiation/immunotherapy agents follow?
options: A) Observation alone; Oral amoxicillin
B) Bilateral nephrectomy; Intravenous insulin
C) Low-dose aspirin; Topical hydrocortisone
D) High-dose chemotherapy with Autologous Stem Cell Rescue (ASCT), followed by 13-cis-retinoic acid (Isotretinoin) and Dinutuximab (anti-GD2) immunotherapy
questions.hint: High-dose chemo + autologous stem cell rescue, followed by 13-cis-retinoic acid and dinutuximab.
questions.explanation: High-risk neuroblastoma (MYCN amplified) requires myeloablative consolidation with Autologous Stem Cell Rescue (ASCT), followed by differentiation therapy (13-cis-retinoic acid) and targeted immunotherapy (Dinutuximab / anti-GD2).

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy has chronic watery diarrhea, muscle weakness from serum potassium 2.1 mmol/L, metabolic acidosis, and a 3 cm right adrenal mass. Which paraneoplastic hormone is hyper-secreted, and what is the diagnosis?
options: A) Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) hypersecretion; Neuroblastoma (Kerner-Morrison syndrome)
B) Renin hypersecretion; Wilms tumor
C) Insulin hypersecretion; Nesidioblastosis
D) Parathyroid hormone hypersecretion; Parathyroid adenoma
questions.hint: VIP hypersecretion causing watery diarrhea and hypokalemia = neuroblastoma (Kerner-Morrison syndrome).
questions.explanation: Secretion of Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) by neuroblastoma causes severe watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (Kerner-Morrison syndrome), which resolves upon tumor resection.

questions.q: For a 3-year-old with a retroperitoneal abdominal mass: what initial imaging confirms location/origin, what urine tests are ordered, and what tissue evaluation finalizes risk classification?
options: A) 1. Plain X-ray of skull; 2. Stool reducing sugars; 3. Skin prick test
B) 1. Chest radiograph only; 2. Serum creatinine; 3. Lumbar puncture

C) 1. Abdominal Ultrasound followed by contrast-enhanced CT/MRI; 2. 24-hour urinary catecholamines (HVA and VMA); 3. Histopathological examination (favorable vs anaplastic histology, MYCN status, WT1 status)
D) 1. Barium swallow; 2. Urine dipstick for glucose; 3. Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear
questions.hint: Ultrasound + CT/MRI, urinary HVA/VMA, and histopathology/molecular testing (anaplasia, MYCN, WT1).
questions.explanation: Definitive evaluation of an abdominal embryonal mass requires Ultrasound and CT/MRI (organ of origin, vascular relations), urinary HVA/VMA (catecholamines for neuroblastoma), and tissue histopathology (evaluating anaplasia, MYCN amplification, or WT1 mutations).
